metadata.title: Understanding teaching professionals' digital competence: What do PIAAC and TALIS reveal about technology-related skills, attitudes, and knowledge?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIAAC (Cycle 1 Round 1) and TALIS 2018 microdata pooled across 11 European countries, but it does not report a specific weight variable name in the provided text. For all computed statistics (distributions, cross-tabulations, correlations, and regression models), the authors state that survey weights were applied to account for the complex sampling designs of PIAAC and TALIS. In the PIAAC skill analyses, they additionally use the PIAAC plausible values methodology (implemented via a SAS macro) to obtain correct uncertainty under the PV framework. The paper does not indicate replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight usage cannot be confirmed from the excerpt; however, the use of survey-weighted procedures implies population-representative estimation rather than an unweighted convenience sample.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper explicitly describes the PV methodology for PIAAC (requiring multiple imputations/combining across PVs), but it does not provide a dedicated description of how missing questionnaire/background data were handled in the regression models (e.g., listwise deletion vs multiple imputation). This is a reporting gap because missingness handling can affect regression coefficients and standard errors, especially when combining PIAAC and TALIS variables and when some respondents did not take the PIAAC test. The authors do report that some PIAAC respondents did not take the test and were merged into the weak-skills group, but they do not generalize this to missingness in other variables.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The authors restrict PIAAC to respondents working as professionals in the education industry using UN ISIC and ILO ISCO industry/occupation classifications, yielding 2590 teaching professionals (with ~93% teachers). They further restrict the overall study to 11 European countries that participated in both PIAAC PS-in-TRE and TALIS 2018, and they pool these countries as a single dataset while controlling for fixed country effects in regression models. For PIAAC skills, they use PS-in-TRE proficiency levels derived from plausible values and merge respondents who did not take the PS-in-TRE test (n=164) into the weak-skills group (levels 0/1), justified by the test being available only digitally and requiring basic computer skills. For TALIS, they use the teacher questionnaire for 50,800 respondents from the same 11 countries, and they analyze only the selected attitude and knowledge items (single items rather than composite scores) for the three clusters.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 (2011-2012) PS-in-TRE skills for teaching professionals (11 European countries pooled)
main_findings.target_variable: PS-in-TRE digital skills proficiency (weak vs strong; PV-based levels)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted logistic regression (country fixed effects). Weak-skills model: Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.13; Strong-skills model: Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.04. Reported odds ratios include: Age (weak OR=1.57; strong OR=0.67), Language background (non-native OR=0.45 for weak), Number of books at home (weak OR=0.80), ICT use at work (weak OR=0.61), ICT use outside work (weak OR=1.40).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 PS-in-TRE data for teaching professionals pooled across 11 European countries, the study leveraged Age group, Language background (native speaker), Number of books at home, ICT use at work, and ICT use outside work to predict PS-in-TRE digital skills proficiency (weak vs strong), finding that higher age increased the probability of weak skills and decreased the probability of strong skills, while ICT use at work was associated with lower odds of weak skills. This indicates that targeting digital-skills support toward older teachers and leveraging workplace ICT use may help reduce weak digital proficiency, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 (2011-2012) background questionnaire for teaching professionals (11 European countries pooled)
main_findings.target_variable: Self-reported possession of computer skills needed at work (attitude indicator)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted logistic regression (country fixed effects). Model fit: R-squared = 0.06 (Nagelkerke). Significant predictors reported in Table 4: Age (OR=1.57 for weak-skills model; for the self-reported skills-needed-at-work outcome, age is not explicitly listed as significant in the excerpted rows, but the text states age, gender, and ICT use outside work are significant). Gender (male OR=2.30), ICT use outside work OR=1.40; coefficients and ORs are shown in Table 4 for the 'Believes to possess the computer skills needed at work' outcome.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 data for teaching professionals pooled across 11 European countries, the study leveraged Age group, Gender, and ICT use outside work to predict self-reported possession of computer skills needed at work, finding that the probability was highest among the youngest respondents, males, and more active ICT users outside work. This indicates that professional development and confidence-building initiatives may need to be tailored by age and gender and should consider teachers’ ICT engagement beyond the workplace, while recognizing that self-reports may not align with measured skills.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire (lower secondary focus; 11 European countries pooled)
main_findings.target_variable: Attitude: ability to support student learning through ICT (single TALIS item)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (country fixed effects). Outcome sample sizes: n=48,189; R-squared = 0.02. Significant predictors in Table 5: Age (b=-0.06), Gender (male b=-0.04), Subject category (Technology b=0.38; Physical education b=-0.38; other subject categories also show significant differences).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data pooled across 11 European countries, the study leveraged Age group, Gender, Educational level (highest degree), and Primary subject taught to predict the attitude item on supporting student learning through ICT, finding that technology teachers reported higher support and physical education teachers reported lower support, with small overall explanatory power (R-squared=0.02). This indicates that subject-specific teacher support and ICT integration strategies may be more effective than one-size-fits-all training, while acknowledging that effects are modest and based on self-reported attitudes.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire (11 European countries pooled)
main_findings.target_variable: Attitude: frequency of letting students use ICT for projects/class work (single TALIS item)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (country fixed effects). Outcome sample sizes: n=38,042; R-squared = 0.03. Significant predictors in Table 5: Age (b=0.02), Gender (male b=-0.08), Subject category (Class teachers b=-0.23; Technology b=0.78; Physical education b=-0.71; Mathematics/science b=-0.25; Languages b=-0.17).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data pooled across 11 European countries, the study leveraged Age group, Gender, Educational level (highest degree), and Primary subject taught to predict the attitude item on how often teachers let students use ICT, finding that technology teachers reported substantially higher ICT use while physical education teachers reported lower use, with low model fit (R-squared=0.03). This indicates that instructional ICT opportunities and coaching should be differentiated by subject area and teacher demographics, though the results reflect associations in self-reported classroom practices rather than causal impacts.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire (11 European countries pooled)
main_findings.target_variable: Attitude: importance of investing in ICT in education (single TALIS item)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (country fixed effects). Outcome sample sizes: n=47,570; R-squared = 0.02. Significant predictors in Table 5: Age (b=0.02), Gender (male b=-0.05), Subject category (Technology b=0.29; Physical education b not shown as significant in excerpted rows but other categories show significant differences; Languages b=-0.07*; Mathematics/science b=-0.05*).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data pooled across 11 European countries, the study leveraged Age group, Gender, Educational level (highest degree), and Primary subject taught to predict the attitude item on the importance of investing in ICT, finding that technology teachers rated ICT investment as more important and that overall explanatory power was small (R-squared=0.02). This indicates that policy messaging and investment rationales may need to be aligned with teachers’ subject contexts to strengthen positive attitudes, while noting that the study does not demonstrate that attitudes cause later ICT integration.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire (11 European countries pooled)
main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge: ICT included in formal education/training (single TALIS item; logistic model)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted logistic regression (country fixed effects). Outcome sample sizes: n=48,970; Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.13. Significant predictors in Table 6: Age (b=-0.64; OR=0.53), Gender (male b=0.30; OR=1.36), Subject category (Technology b=0.40; OR=1.48; Physical education b=-0.73; OR=0.48; Languages b=-0.41; OR=0.67; Mathematics/science b=0.22; OR=1.25).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data pooled across 11 European countries, the study leveraged Age group, Gender, Educational level (highest degree), and Primary subject taught to predict whether ICT was included in teachers’ formal education/training, finding that younger teachers and male teachers were more likely to report ICT inclusion and that technology teachers reported the highest inclusion. This indicates that curriculum design in teacher education programs may be a key lever for building digital-technology knowledge, especially for older teachers and non-technology subject groups.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire (11 European countries pooled)
main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge: feeling prepared for using ICT in teaching (single TALIS item; linear model)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (country fixed effects). Outcome sample sizes: n=46,970; R-squared = 0.11. Significant predictors in Table 6: Age (b=-0.23; OR=0.53 shown in table), Gender (male b=0.20; OR=1.09), Subject category (Technology b=0.52; OR=1.48; Physical education b=-0.27; OR=0.76; Languages b=-0.14; OR=0.67; Mathematics/science b not significant in excerpted rows).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data pooled across 11 European countries, the study leveraged Age group, Gender, and Primary subject taught to predict teachers’ feeling prepared to use ICT in teaching, finding that preparation decreases with age and is higher among technology teachers, with moderate model fit (R-squared=0.11). This indicates that targeted preparation and confidence-building for older teachers and subject groups with lower preparedness may be necessary to support digital transformation in classrooms.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire (11 European countries pooled)
main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge: need for professional development in ICT skills (single TALIS item; linear model)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted linear regression (country fixed effects). Outcome sample sizes: n=48,453; R-squared = 0.03. Significant predictors in Table 6: Age (b=0.09; OR=1.12), Gender (male b=-0.12; OR=0.89), Subject category (Class teachers b=0.24; OR=1.26; Languages b=0.09; OR=1.09; Technology b not significant in excerpted rows; Physical education b=0.14; OR=1.03).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data pooled across 11 European countries, the study leveraged Age group, Gender, and Primary subject taught to predict teachers’ need for professional development in ICT skills, finding that the need increases with age and is higher for some subject groups (e.g., class teachers) while males report lower need. This indicates that professional development planning should prioritize older teachers and specific subject areas, while recognizing that the low R-squared suggests substantial unmeasured variation in training needs.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire (11 European countries pooled)
main_findings.target_variable: Knowledge: participation in ICT-related professional development activities during last 12 months (single TALIS item; logistic model)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Survey-weighted logistic regression (country fixed effects). Outcome sample sizes: n=46,804; Nagelkerke R-squared = 0.01. Significant predictors in Table 6: Gender (male b=-0.12; OR=1.20 shown in table), Subject category (Class teachers b=0.23; OR=1.26; Languages b=0.33; OR=1.39; Technology b not significant in excerpted rows; Physical education b not significant in excerpted rows).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data pooled across 11 European countries, the study leveraged Age group, Gender, and Primary subject taught to predict participation in ICT-related professional development activities, finding very low explanatory power (Nagelkerke R-squared=0.01) and limited but detectable differences by gender and subject category. This indicates that simply identifying training needs may not translate into actual participation, so policy should address structural barriers to access and uptake of ICT professional development.

data.outcome_summary: The study pools PIAAC Cycle 1 Round 1 (2011–2012) PS-in-TRE data and TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data from 11 European countries to examine digital competence of teaching professionals as three clusters: measured skills, self-reported attitudes, and self-reported knowledge. For PIAAC skills, it uses PV-based proficiency levels (weak vs strong) and survey-weighted logistic regression with country fixed effects; the weak-skills model shows Nagelkerke R-squared=0.13 and the strong-skills model R-squared=0.04. For TALIS attitudes and knowledge, it uses survey-weighted regression models on single items (because correlations were too low for reliable composites), with R-squared values around 0.02–0.11 for attitudes and knowledge, and Nagelkerke R-squared=0.13 for ICT inclusion in formal education. The best-supported predictors across models are age and subject category (especially technology vs physical education). Limitations include correlational design, reliance on self-reports for attitudes/knowledge, and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling beyond PV methodology.
